video_title: Scaling Laws: Matt Abrams on Trust and the Migration to the Digital Age
gist: Matt Abrams argues the U.S. faces a compounding, cross-institutional trust collapse because a physical-world constitution has been silently replaced by digital terms of service, and that the AI opportunity lies not in generative slop but in civic-engineering tools (deliberation tech, citizen assemblies, policy simulation) that rebuild agency and trust from the local level up.

insights.claim: Public sentiment toward AI among younger Americans is overwhelmingly negative: 61% of under-30 adults expect AI to worsen creative thinking, 58% expect it to erode meaningful relationships, and only 14% expect net-positive societal effects.
insights.speaker: Kevin (host)
insights.so_what: Consumer-facing AI firms face a demand-side legitimacy problem with the youngest cohort; brand and adoption risk is understated in valuations premised on universal enthusiasm.
insights.quote: 61% say that AI is going to worsen people's ability to think creatively. 58% say it's going to erode their capacity to form meaningful relationships. And just 14% of adults under 30 expect AI's effects to be positive on society.

insights.claim: Only 15% of Americans trust AI companies to make decisions about how AI is developed, and only 17% trust the federal government to do what is right, indicating that neither industry self-governance nor state regulation currently commands public legitimacy.
insights.speaker: Kevin (host)
insights.so_what: A dual-legitimacy vacuum raises the probability of reactive, populist regulation of AI; watch for bottom-up/local governance experiments as the credible alternative.
insights.quote: only 15% of Americans say they trust AI companies to make decisions about how AI is developed and used.

insights.claim: Generalized interpersonal trust has fallen to roughly 34% of Americans, meaning the erosion is not confined to institutions but extends to citizen-to-citizen relationships.
insights.speaker: Kevin (host)
insights.so_what: Low baseline social trust is a structural headwind for any platform, marketplace, or product whose value depends on strangers cooperating; trust-infrastructure is an emerging category.
insights.quote: only 34% of Americans say that most people can be trusted.

insights.claim: The current distrust episode is distinct from Watergate because trust is collapsing simultaneously across all institutions rather than in one domain, amid an information-flood ('flood the zone') that outpaces humans' evolved capacity to interrogate information.
insights.speaker: Matt Abrams
insights.so_what: Simultaneous multi-institution failure means point solutions won't restore trust; the investable opportunity is cross-cutting epistemic infrastructure, not single-vertical fixes.
insights.quote: everything across society is is losing trust you know simultaneously

themes.theme: Digital Border Control and the Terms-of-Service Constitution

insights.claim: The physical-world U.S. Constitution has effectively been replaced by corporate terms of service in the digital realm, stripping citizens of digital-home privacy without any comparable constitutional protection.
insights.speaker: Matt Abrams
insights.so_what: Frames a coming regulatory battleground over digital property/privacy rights; firms whose business models depend on frictionless data capture carry latent legal-regime risk.
insights.quote: that has effectively in my mind been replaced with with terms of service in the digital world

insights.claim: Cloud and AI providers face no requirement or economic incentive to impose 'digital border control' on who signs up, because they have sunk enormous capex into data centers and must monetize usage regardless of the user's origin or intent.
insights.speaker: Matt Abrams
insights.so_what: Export-control and national-security pressure could force costly KYC/geo-screening onto cloud and frontier-AI providers, a margin and compliance overhang worth watching.
insights.quote: they don't have any requirement or economic incentive to block the users who sign up for their cloud services

insights.claim: Roughly one in eight applications used by military service members has been found to contain foreign (e.g., Chinese) code, which Abrams frames as the modern 'quartering of soldiers' in citizens' digital homes.
insights.speaker: Matt Abrams
insights.so_what: App-provenance and software-bill-of-materials scrutiny is a growth vector; procurement rules could rapidly disadvantage apps with foreign code dependencies.
insights.quote: one in eight applications for military service members uh um evidently have been found to have foreign code from China

insights.claim: There are effectively more licensing requirements to be a beautician in California than to be a software developer, despite software now being critical infrastructure and citizens' 'new home.'
insights.speaker: Matt Abrams
insights.so_what: Signals building momentum toward software-developer accountability/liability standards; secure-by-design and software-liability regimes are a plausible regulatory frontier.
insights.quote: there are more requirements to be a butician in the state of California than there are to be a software developer

insights.claim: Open-source AI and the Export Control Reform Act are converging into an emerging fight over whether cloud-hosted models can be restricted from non-U.S. users, extending physical border-control logic into the digital domain.
insights.speaker: Kevin (host)
insights.so_what: Cloud-delivered model access is the likely next node for export-control policy; providers of frontier and open-weight models face jurisdictional access-restriction risk.

themes.theme: Corporate Legitimacy and the AI Narrative Deficit

insights.claim: Corporations historically had to demonstrate a public-good purpose to obtain a charter and were tied to the powers of the state; that public-purpose requirement has disappeared, weakening any alignment between corporate ends and the public interest.
insights.speaker: Matt Abrams / Kevin (host)
insights.so_what: Revives a case for public-benefit obligations; expect renewed scrutiny of AI firms' stated missions and possible pressure toward public-benefit or chartered structures.
insights.quote: It used to be a requirement for to be a corporation. You had to show what you were doing for the public good.

insights.claim: AI companies' articulation of what they are building for is vague and imprecise, defaulting to lofty promises like 'cure cancer,' which fails to build public trust and invites backlash when the concrete deliverable is perceived as 'slop' requiring local data centers and personal data.
insights.speaker: Kevin (host)
insights.so_what: Narrative and tangible-benefit deficits are a real permitting and social-license risk for AI infrastructure buildout; firms that tie output to felt public benefit reduce siting and regulatory friction.
insights.quote: their annunciation of what they're actually building for is incredibly imprecise, very vague

insights.claim: The tech industry preached 'software and STEM' as the only viable livelihood, denigrating trades, and is now reversing into a 'software developer apocalypse'—a whiplash that has destroyed trust because the industry told the public one thing and then delivered another.
insights.speaker: Matt Abrams
insights.so_what: Credibility whiplash fuels worker distrust and political risk for AI-driven automation; reskilling narratives that lack follow-through will not defuse opposition.
insights.quote: now we're going to have the software developer apocalypse

insights.claim: Engineers systematically fail at storytelling—there are many Wozniaks but few Jobs—so AI's benefits are communicated in ways that do not resonate with lumber workers, coal miners, farmers, or doctors, breeding a sense of imposed technology and lost agency.
insights.speaker: Matt Abrams
insights.so_what: The gap between technical capability and mainstream narrative is a monetizable niche (translation, communications, civic-facing product design) and a leading indicator of adoption friction.
insights.quote: we have a lot of Steve Waznjaks running around, but not many Steve Jobs. And without Steve Jobs, there would be no Apple.

insights.claim: Users increasingly experience 'plastic freedom'—abundance of choice within digital platforms that masks a real loss of agency over privacy, data ownership, and algorithmic choice—which began with social media and is amplified by AI.
insights.speaker: Matt Abrams
insights.so_what: Demand for user agency (data rights, algorithmic choice) is an unmet market; products granting genuine control could differentiate against incumbents in a low-trust environment.
insights.quote: instead they're feeling plastic freedom

insights.claim: Statistically representative citizen/civic assemblies—'jury duty for civic issues' but demographically matched to the community—demonstrably build trust and are already being run on real issues (youth homelessness in central Oregon, property taxes in Connecticut).
insights.speaker: Matt Abrams
insights.so_what: Deliberation/civic-assembly tooling is a nascent govtech category with proven local traction; watch operators building the software and facilitation layer.
insights.quote: think jury duty for for issues and it's civic issues

insights.claim: Today's engagement algorithms lock users in belief-reinforcing bubbles, and the deliberate design alternative is 'bridging algorithms' that reward healthy cross-cutting dialogue instead of incentivizing the 'village idiots.'
insights.speaker: Matt Abrams
insights.so_what: Bridging-algorithm and deliberation platforms (DemNext, Google Jigsaw, Polis) are named leaders in a space that could attract regulatory tailwinds and institutional buyers.
insights.quote: right now we have algorithms which are putting us in our bubbles and our silos and reinforcing our belief systems

insights.claim: A major untapped AI application is a 'SimCity 2.0' for governance—simulating the intended and unintended consequences of proposed legislation before enactment, the way AI is already used in drug discovery.
insights.speaker: Matt Abrams / Kevin (host)
insights.so_what: Policy/legislative simulation is a whitespace application of improving AI simulation capability; early movers could define a new 'regulatory technology' category and public-sector procurement line.
insights.quote: imagine if if whether it's our you know existing representatives so on so forth could actually... are we actually going to get the intended unintended consequences of that

insights.claim: AI's strongest and continually improving capability is simulation, and future generations will find it bizarre that legislatures did not simulate likely legislative outcomes—potentially gating passage on achieving stated outcomes or requiring supermajorities otherwise.
insights.speaker: Kevin (host)
insights.so_what: Points to demand for outcome-simulation as a procedural governance requirement; a forward market for civic-simulation vendors if any jurisdiction mandates it.
insights.quote: why the hell were you not mandating that your legislature simulate the likely outcomes of that piece of legislation?

insights.claim: 'AI' should not be conflated with LLMs/generative models; the civic-engineering opportunity spans a broader toolkit (simulation, bridging systems) beyond transformer-based generative AI.
insights.speaker: Matt Abrams
insights.so_what: Reminds investors that value in civic and simulation applications may accrue to non-generative AI methods, not just the frontier-LLM narrative.
insights.quote: AI is not just LLMs. It's not just transformer models. It's there's a lot more beyond it

themes.theme: Political Representation and the Geographic Trust Fracture

insights.claim: American representation has degraded from a 'trustee' model to a 'delegate' model and now to a 'personal delegate' model, where constituents support officials only when they mirror the constituent's own personal values regardless of majority or community interest.
insights.speaker: Kevin (host)
insights.so_what: This atomization of democratic expectations predicts continued governance gridlock and volatility—macro-political risk relevant to policy-sensitive sectors.
insights.quote: a model of uh what some people call a personal delegate model of representation where people will only support what their elected official does if it's what they want them to do

insights.claim: The 'Greater Idaho' secession movement—eastern Oregon seeking to join Idaho—is driven by a legitimate representation grievance against Portland and Salem, illustrating that geographic distrust reflects real unaddressed under-representation.
insights.speaker: Matt Abrams
insights.so_what: Secession/regional-grievance movements are a barometer of institutional distrust; useful signal for political-risk mapping in the U.S. interior West.
insights.quote: the eastern portion of the state uh wants to secede to Idaho in part because they don't trust Portland

insights.claim: Technological paradigms are splitting political communities apart: in San Francisco 'spinning up agents' is routine, while in Morgantown, West Virginia the same phrase is unintelligible, threatening the cohesion implied by 'these United States.'
insights.speaker: Kevin (host)
insights.so_what: A widening AI-literacy divide is a durable adoption and political-backlash variable; geographic segmentation matters for both product rollout and regulatory sentiment.
insights.quote: I go and I travel to Morgantown, West Virginia, and if I said spinning up agents, they would look like I just had 15 Mountain Dews

insights.claim: The three defining features of republican government per Federalist 10—deliberation, cooling of impassioned response, and countering factions—could be scaled by AI to entire communities, an option unavailable to 18th-century framers.
insights.speaker: Kevin (host)
insights.so_what: Reframes AI as an enabler of scaled deliberation, supporting the civic-tech thesis and a governance-tooling market rather than merely an automation threat.
insights.quote: how can AI actually advance the core aspects of republican governance rather than advance republican governance as we know it today

insights.claim: Formative in-person civic experiences are irreplaceable: even a perfect value-aligned AI cannot supply the social 'glue' that binds a political community, so human-to-human engagement remains a prerequisite for trust.
insights.speaker: Kevin (host)
insights.so_what: Bounds the total addressable market for purely digital civic solutions; blended human+AI models are more defensible than fully automated deliberation.
insights.quote: even if we had an AI model that could perfectly express our values and beliefs... then we still don't have that glue that binds us all together as a political community

insights.claim: Abrams endorses mandatory national service—broadly defined as service, not only military—arguing people are hungry for purpose and contribution, and proposes an 'army of civic engineers' to build new institutions for the digital age.
insights.speaker: Matt Abrams
insights.so_what: A national-service push would create demand for civic-tech and training infrastructure; signals the direction advocates want policy and philanthropy to fund.
insights.quote: I want to see an army of civic engineers that is helping build the new country.

insights.claim: Had frontier AI labs partnered on a tangible, felt public moonshot (e.g., cancer) rather than shipping deepfakes and novelty video, the AI–data-center backlash would be materially reduced because trust follows visible, real-world benefit.
insights.speaker: Matt Abrams
insights.so_what: Directs where AI firms should concentrate flagship efforts to earn social license; visible health/science wins are a strategic hedge against infrastructure opposition.
insights.quote: let's solve real problems that affect everyday people that people can feel and touch and understand and make their lives better and your narrative is then solved for you.

insights.claim: New institutions such as data trusts and data co-ops—'give us your data and we'll build tools for you'—could be transformative by giving citizens collective ownership and leverage over their data.
insights.speaker: Kevin (host)
insights.so_what: Data-trust/co-op structures are an emerging institutional model to watch as a counterweight to platform data monopolies and a potential new asset class.
insights.quote: having new institutions like data trusts and data co-ops that say give us your data and then we'll build tools for you would be so transformative
